D:\\wt\\skhpapers\\vlog\\skhpapers\\voz\.text: Open the drawer, dear, you know the one, the kitchen drawer that does not close all the way, or the box in the hall closet that says important in your own handwriting from 20 years ago. Now imagine your daughter opening it after you are gone. She will sit on the floor with a garbage bag, and 9 out of every 10 pieces of paper will go into that bag without being read. I know this because I did it to my mother. In Osaka, in two weeks, my brother and I carried out 41 bags of paper from a house of three small rooms. And somewhere in those bags, I am almost sure, was something she wanted me to keep. I will never know what it was. That is the part that still wakes me up some nights. Not the mess. The one thing I lost inside the mess. So today I am going to give you the 11 Japanese rules I follow at 80, so my children will not have to do what I did.

Where to start, what to keep, the one blue folder that matters more than every drawer in the house, and what to do with the letters you cannot throw away. Rule number seven is the one my neighbor Doris did not believe until she tried it. And rule number eleven is the one almost nobody does, and it is the one that would have saved me those two weeks in Osaka. Before we start, dear, if you are new here, press subscribe and the little bell. Every week I bring you one more Japanese way to keep a home light and calm. And I want to ask you one question and you can answer it in the comments. What is the oldest piece of paper in your house? Mine is a train ticket from 1958. I will tell you about it later. Now, let us open the drawer. You know me. I am Sachiko. I came to America in 1970 and I have kept this little house for 50 years. Thank you.

In Japan we have a word for this work, Seizen Seiri. It means putting your things in order while you are still alive. It is not a sad word. It is a kind word. It means you love the people who will come after you enough to do the hard part yourself. My mother, Fumiko, lived in the same house in Osaka for 62 years. It had tatami mats, paper sliding doors, and a tall wooden chest of drawers we call a tansu, made of polonia wood, with iron handles that clicked when you let them go. When she passed in 2003, my brother Kenji and I opened that tansu. Every drawer was paper, newspapers folded in four, New Year cards tied with string, electric bills from the 1960s, manuals for a rice cooker she had given away before I was married. And under all of it, in the bottom drawer, a brown envelope that said nothing on the front. I almost put it in the bag.

I will tell you what was inside at the end. Here is what I learned on the floor of that house. Paper is the heaviest thing we leave behind, not the furniture. Furniture you call a truck, and it is gone in one afternoon. Paper must be read, one page at a time, because one page in a thousand matters. That is why your children will throw away ninety percent of it. They do not have the time to read it, and they are afraid of it, and they are grieving. So they throw it all and they hope. My 11 rules are how I make sure the 10% they keep is the right 10%. Rule number 1. Start with the paper that has no story. Most people start with the hardest thing, the box of letters from their husband or the children's report cards. They sit down at the table with one letter and two hours later they are crying and nothing has left the house. Paper with a story stops you.

So you begin with paper that nobody will ever miss. Magazines, catalogs, flyers from the grocery store, old newspapers you were saving for the one article you will never read again, envelopes from the bank that are only advertising. My mother kept the Asahi newspaper by the door of the genkan, the little entry where we leave our shoes, a stack as tall as my knee, tied with plastic string, every month. She said she was saving it for wrapping. She wrapped maybe ten things a year. The stack grew for forty years. Here is how I do it now. One grocery bag. A kitchen timer for fifteen minutes, only fifteen. I walk through the house and pick up every magazine, every catalogue, every flyer, and I do not open them. I do not read the cover. If I start reading, I lose.

When the timer rings, the bag goes straight to the recycling bin outside, not to the garage, not to the porch, outside, that same minute. The first time I did this, I filled three bags in 15 minutes, and I felt 10 years younger. The mistake almost everybody makes here is to keep the magazine for one recipe or for one article. Dear, if you want one page, tear out the one page right now and put it in a single folder called to read. the rest of the magazine goes. And if the to read folder is full, you are not going to read it. Be honest with yourself. I was not honest for many years. Rule number two. Paper does not cross the Genkan without a decision. In Japan, the Genkan is the line between the outside world and your home. You take off your shoes there because the dirt of the street stays outside. I do the same with the mail. Every day, I open the mail standing at the door. Thank you.

I do not carry it to the kitchen table. The kitchen table is where paper goes to sleep for ten years. By the door I keep three things. A small basket, a paper bag for recycling, and a letter opener my husband Tom gave me in 1980. Advertising goes into the paper bag without opening. Envelopes, I must answer, go into the basket. That is all. Two minutes a day. On Sunday afternoon I sit down with the basket and a cup of Genmaicha, and I answer everything in it, and the basket is empty again for Monday. My mother had no basket. Her mail went everywhere, on the shoe shelf, under the telephone, inside the rice bowl cupboard. When we cleaned her house, we found an unopened letter from her own sister, from 1991. Her sister had passed in 94. I sat in the genkan and read it to my brother out loud. It was only about the weather and a new grandchild.

but my mother never read it. Two minutes a day, dear. Two minutes at the door would have given her that letter. And here is what I do now at 80. When something important arrives that I do not understand, a letter from the bank, from the insurance, from the city, I do not guess. I put it in the basket with a yellow sticky note that says, Ask. On Sunday, I call my son, or I call the office on the letter. I am not a lawyer, and I am not an accountant. I am a grandmother with a shredder. The people whose job it is to know, they know. I only know how to make sure the letter does not get lost. Now, Rules 1 and 2 keep new paper from piling up, but you still have the old drawer, the one we opened at the beginning. Rule 3 empties half of it in one afternoon, and it is the rule my children laughed at, until they saw how much of the drawer was gone. Rule Number 3. The manuals go.

All of them. Almost. In every house in America, there is a drawer of instruction books. The blender. The microwave. The television you replaced in 2009. The garage door opener from the house you sold. I counted mine the first time. 56 manuals, dear. For maybe 20 machines that still lived in my house. My mother had the same drawer in Osaka. In the bottom of the kitchen cabinet. it, with the manual for a washing machine she threw away in 1985, still in its plastic bag. She kept the manual for thirty years after the machine was gone. When I asked my brother why she did that, he said, in case. In case of what? Nobody knew. That is the voice of paper. In case. Here is how I sort them. First, any manual for a machine that is no longer in the house goes immediately.

I walk from room to room with the drawer in my arms like a waitress with a tray, and I check. If the machine is not there, the manual goes in the bag. Second for the machines I still have, my grandson showed me that almost every manual is on the company website, for free. He wrote the model numbers on a single sheet of paper for me, one line per machine. That one sheet lives in the blue folder, which I will tell you about in Rule 6. The books go. I keep only two kinds of manuals in paper. The ones for things that keep me safe and that I touch rarely, like the furnace or the smoke alarm, so the repairman and my children can find them in a hurry, and the ones with the little card that has the warranty, while the warranty is still alive. I staple the receipt to the front page so the proof and the book live together. When the warranty ends, the manual goes too.

The mistake people make with manuals is keeping the box, too. Oh, the boxes. Cardboard boxes in the garage for a computer from 2012. Your children will open every one of those boxes, hoping something is inside, and nothing will be inside. Please, do not make them do that. Rule number four. A receipt has a short life, and you decide its life the day you get it. In my mother's tansu we found receipts from 1964. The ink had faded to nothing. You could not read the store, the price, or the date. Just thin white paper, curled like a dry leaf. She kept every one, because she grew up after the war. And after the war, paper meant proof, and proof meant safety. I understand her, but I do it differently. On my refrigerator I have one clear plastic pocket with a magnet. Every receipt from the week goes in that pocket.

On Sunday, with my jenmaicha and the basket from the jenkan, I take the receipts out and I look at each one for three seconds. Is it for something I might return? It stays one more month. Is it for something with a warranty? It gets stapled to the manual, like I told you. Is it for groceries, gas, the pharmacy, coffee with Doris? Into the shredder. Now, dear, for the papers that have to do with taxes and money and the law, I do not decide alone and you should not decide because a grandmother on YouTube told you How long to keep them is a question for your accountant or the tax office in your own country? Because the rules are not the same everywhere and they change what I can tell you is how I store them one accordion folder one pocket per year and on the front of each pocket the year in big black numbers and

When my accountant tells me a year can go, the whole pocket goes into the shredder, at once, without reading. No digging. No sorting the same paper twice. The mistake here is the shoebox. One shoebox becomes four shoeboxes, and nobody, not you, not your children, not the accountant, can find anything in four shoeboxes. A receipt that cannot be found is the same as no receipt. It is only weight. So far we have cleared magazines, mail, manuals, and receipts. That is the easy paper. Rule 5 is where most people stop, because now the paper starts to have faces on it. And I want to show you how my mother's New Year cards taught me the gentlest way to let paper go. Rule number 5. Keep the person, not the pile of cards. In Japan, every New Year, we send cards called Nengajo. small postcards with the animal of the year, a short greeting, sometimes a photo of the family.

The post office keeps them and delivers them all on the morning of January 1st, so the whole country opens its mailbox at the same time. It is a beautiful tradition, and it is a mountain of paper. My mother kept every nengaro she received for over 50 years. They were tied in bundles with red string, one bundle per year, in a wooden box on top of the tansu. Thousands of cards. When we opened the box, my brother sighed so loudly the neighbor's dog started barking. But here is what I discovered, kneeling on the tatami with those bundles. Most of the cards were printed. The same picture, the same greeting, a printed name. Only some of them had a few words written by hand. Your plum tree must be blooming soon. I think of your mother every winter. Those handwritten lines were my mother's real friendships. The rest was the post office.

So this is my rule now, for Christmas cards, birthday cards, New Year cards, all of them. When the season is over, I read every card one more time. If it is only printed, I say thank you, out loud, I really do say it, and it goes in the recycling. If it has handwriting, I keep only the best one from each person, one card per person, not one card per year. I keep them in a single box, the size of a shoebox, no bigger. If the box is full, a new card can come in only if an old one leaves. And the addresses, I copy into one small address book, so the cards do not have to stay just to remember where my friends live. The mistake is thinking that throwing away the card is throwing away the friend. It is not. My friend Michiko in Kobe has sent me a card every year since 1966. I keep one card from her.

The one from the year my husband died, where she wrote, Now you must eat for both of you. That one card holds 50 years of Michiko. The other 49 cards were only paper. Rule number six. One blue folder. This is the most important paper in your house, and most houses do not have it. When my mother died, we did not know where anything was. Which bank, which insurance, where the papers for the house were, who to call about the pension. We spent the first four days not grieving, but searching, opening drawers, calling offices, saying, I am her daughter, I am sorry, I do not know her account number. Four days, dear, four days I should have spent sitting with my brother, remembering her. So I have one folder. It is blue because blue is easy to say on the telephone. Look for the blue folder in the top drawer of my desk. Everybody can find blue.

Inside the folder is not money advice. I do not give money advice. Inside the folder is a map, one page that says where things are, not the secrets themselves, just the places. On my page there is a list, the names of the people who helped me, my doctor, my accountant, the lawyer who helped Tom and me years ago, my insurance agent with their telephone numbers, the names of the companies where I have an account or a policy, but not the passwords and not the numbers, only the names, so my children know who to call, where the original important papers are kept, like the papers of the house, the car, the marriage certificate, Tom's papers, the sheet with the model numbers of my machines, from Rule 3, and the name of the person I trust most to help my children if they feel lost.

which papers are important and how they must be prepared. That is a question for a lawyer in your own state or country, and I really mean that. I am only telling you about the folder. Twice a year, on New Year's Day and on my birthday in June, I take out the blue folder and I read my one page and I fix what changed. A new doctor, a closed account, a new phone number, 10 minutes, And then I call my son and my daughter and I say, the blue folder is in the same place. They roll their eyes, but they know. The mistake with the blue folder is making it too fat. If you put every paper in it, it becomes another drawer and nobody will read it. The blue folder is thin, a map, not the treasure, 10 pages at most. And the first page tells everything. Now, rule 7. This is the one Doris did not believe. She is my neighbor, 83, and she has a basement full of letters.

And when I told her rule 7, she said, Sachiko, that is cruel. Two weeks later, she called me and said, I cannot stop doing it. But first, one second, dear. If these rules are helping you, press subscribe and the little bell. Because next week, I will show you the Japanese way to empty a whole closet in one weekend without crying. And tell me in the comments, who is the person in your family who will open your drawers one day? just their first name. I like to read them and I say a little thank you for each one. Rule number seven, read the letters once more and then choose ten. Letters are the hardest paper, love letters, letters from your mother, from a son in the army, from a friend who moved away. You cannot throw them away and you should not throw them all away, but a box of 300 letters will be thrown away whole, unopened by tired hands. That is the truth.

Your children cannot read 300 letters in a weekend, so they will read none. My mother kept every letter my father wrote her during the two years he worked in Nagoya before they were married. A hundred and eighty letters, we found them in the tansu, under the receipts. My brother wanted to burn them all. He said they were private. I wanted to keep them all. We argued in the garden until the sun went down. In the end we kept them all, and they are in my closet in America, and I have never read them. Forty-one bags of paper, and the hundred and eighty letters I kept, I am afraid to open. So here is rule seven, and here is why Doris said it was cruel. Once a week, on a quiet evening, I read some letters, slowly, with tea. I let myself remember, and from each person I choose the letters that sound most like them. The ones that make me laugh or cry or that say something true.

At the end, I keep no more than ten letters from each person. The best ten. Those ten go in a polonia box, a kiri box, like the one we keep precious kimono in, because polonia keeps out moisture and insects. On top of the box, I write who the letters are from. The letters that leave, I thank them. In Japan, we have ceremonies to thank old things before we let them go. Dolls, needles, brushes. I do a very small one, only me. I hold the bundle. I say thank you for keeping this for me. And then they go to the shredder. Not the trash, the shredder, because they are private. Doris told me the first evening she cried. The second evening she laughed. And the third evening she read her ten best letters from her husband to her granddaughter on the phone. That is the difference. Ten letters get read. Three hundred letters get thrown. And now I am doing it with my father's letters, slowly.

20 letters a month. I chose 8 so far. In one of them he says my mother's handwriting is like a small bird walking in the snow. I did not know my father could write like that. I would have died without knowing it if I had kept all 180 in the box. Rule number 8. Give the children their childhood back now while you can see their faces. Every mother has this box. the drawings with the purple sun, the report cards, the certificate for swimming 25 meters, the little card that says, to the best mama in the world, with world spelled wrong. We keep these because they are our children's childhood, and we were there. My mother kept my childhood too, my school notebooks from the 1950s with my practice characters 100 times the same kanji, the teacher's red circles, my first calligraphy,

And here I can tell you about my oldest piece of paper, the train ticket. My first train ticket alone, from Osaka to Kyoto, 1958, when I was 12, to visit my aunt. My mother kept it in an envelope with my name. I found it on the tatami, among the 41 bags, and I sat there holding it, crying, because I remembered the whole day. The cold window, the rice ball my mother wrapped for me And I thought, why did she not give me this while she was alive? I would have loved to hear her tell me about that day What was she thinking, waiting at the station? Was she afraid? I will never know, because I found the ticket instead of receiving it So this is rule 8 Take the box of each child Choose the best things Maybe 20 pieces A few drawings one report card, the misspelled card. Put them in a big envelope with their name and give it to them.

in person if you can, at a dinner, at a birthday, and tell them the stories. You drew this the week your grandfather visited. Watch their faces. My son laughed for an hour with his drawings. My daughter cried and then took photos of everything and sent them to her own children. The rest of the box, the hundred other drawings, I asked them first, and they said, Mom, keep only what you love. So I did. The mistake is waiting. We wait because we think the box is for after, but after it is only a box. Now it is a conversation. A box opened with you is a gift. A box opened without you is homework. Now we have three rules left, and they are about the papers that are only yours, your diaries, your someday pile, and the one letter almost nobody writes. Rule 9 is about my mother's notebooks and why it was the one decision I am glad she made by herself. Rule number 9.

Decide yourself what happens to your diaries and notebooks. Do not leave this decision to your children. It is too heavy for them. My mother kept a small notebook every year for 50 years. A kakebo, the Japanese household notebook, where the woman of the house writes every day what she spent on rice, on fish, on school shoes, and at the end of the month, a few lines about how the month went. 50 notebooks in a row on a shelf, thin, with cloth covers. And this is the one thing she did right. Inside the first notebook, on the first page, she wrote a short note. It said, Kenji and Sachiko, keep the notebooks from the year each of you was born, and the year your father died. Burn the rest. They are only numbers and complaints. I love you. So we did exactly that. We kept three notebooks.

And because she told us, there was no fighting, no guilt, no box in my closet I am afraid to open. We burned the others in the garden, in the old iron drum, and my brother and I read lines out loud before each one went into the fire. March 1972. The price of cabbage is a scandal. We laughed until we cried. So for your diaries, your journals, your notebooks, your calendars, where you wrote birthdays for 40 years, You have three choices, and you should choose one now. One, keep them and write on the box what you want done with them. Two, choose the few that matter and let the others go yourself. Three, if they are very private, let them go yourself, with your own hands, while you can decide. I chose two. I kept my diaries from the year I arrived in America and the year Tom died. I wrote a note on the box, like my mother did.

The others I let go, one per evening, last winter. The mistake is to think they will want to read everything. Maybe one child will. But most children open a diary, read one page that is too private or too sad, and close it forever, and then they cannot throw it away and cannot read it. That is the worst kind of paper. A note on the box takes two minutes and saves them 20 years of that. Rule number 10. The Sunday pile gets one shelf and the shelf has a date. Everybody has a Sunday pile. Recipes cut from the newspaper, instructions for a quilt pattern, a brochure for a cruise to Alaska, articles about vitamins, about gardening, about places to visit, papers for a project we will start when we have time. My Sunday pile was three boxes in the spare room. Three. When I finally sat down with them, I found the same recipe for lemon cake cut out four times from four different years

I had forgotten I already cut it. Four times I wanted to bake that cake and I never baked it. That told me everything about my Someday pile. Here is the rule now. The Someday paper lives on one shelf in the spare room no more. Each paper on that shelf gets a date written in the corner with a pencil, the day I put it there. On New Year's Day and on my birthday, the same days I read the blue folder, I look at the shelf. Anything that has been there more than one year and I did not touch it, it goes. It was not someday. It was never. And then I did something my daughter loved. The lemon cake recipe. I baked it. That same week, I invited Doris and two other neighbors and we ate the whole cake and then I threw the four recipes away with a smile. So for each pile, ask yourself, can I do this this month? If yes, do it. If no, let it go.

Some days the best way to clean a paper is to finally do what it says. The mistake is keeping some day paper because it makes you feel like the person who will do it. I kept the Alaska brochure for nine years because I liked being the woman who would go to Alaska. I am not going to Alaska, dear. I am 80 and my knees prefer my garden. The brochure was not a plan. It was a costume. And now, rule 11. The one almost nobody does, the one I promised you at the beginning, and the one that would have saved my brother and me those 2 weeks and 41 bags in Osaka. But first, I want to give you the 5 mistakes I see the most, because maybe you are making one of them right now, the same as I did. Mistake number 1. Sorting by stacks on the floor.

You make a stack for keep, a stack for maybe, a stack for go, and then the phone rings and the stacks stay on the floor for three months. Use bags and boxes, never stacks. A bag can be carried out. A stack only grows. Mistake number two, doing everything in one weekend. You will be tired and sad by Saturday night, and on Sunday you will put everything back. 15 minutes a day is better than a weekend once a year. Paper is patient. You must be more patient. Mistake number three, scanning everything. People buy a scanner. They scan 300 pages, and then they have 300 pages in a computer nobody can open. Scanning is good for a few precious things. It is not a way to keep everything. It only moves the drawer to a place your children cannot find. Mistake number four, throwing private papers into the normal trash.

Anything with your name, your address, your numbers, your signature goes into the shredder. My little shredder costs $30 and it is the best friend I have in this house, after Doris. Mistake number five. Doing it in secret. You clean the drawers, you make the blue folder, and you never tell anybody. Then it is like you did nothing. Tell your children. Tell one person you trust. The best order in the world is useless if nobody knows where the door is. And let me tell you three things my mother never did and I wish she had. She never said no to paper at the door. Every flyer, every free calendar from the fish shop came inside. She never asked for help because she was proud and so she was alone with the tansu for 20 years. And she never told us what was important, except one time, one brown envelope. And that is rule 11. Rule number 11.

Write the letter that tells them which 10% to keep. In Japan, many older people now keep what we call an ending note. It is a notebook, not a legal paper, just a notebook, where you write down your wishes and your story for your family in your own words. The lawyer does the legal part. The ending note does the human part. I do not have a fancy notebook. I have one letter, written by hand, two pages, in an envelope that says, Open this first, in big letters. It lives on top of the blue folder, and it says the most important thing that no folder can say, what I want them to keep. Not everything. My children will throw away 90%. I know that, and I am at peace with that. My letter tells them which 10%. The Kiribok's with the 10 letters from Tom. The Three Kakebo Notebooks of My Mother, my train ticket from 1958, with the story written on the back.

The one card from Michiko, my mother's wooden rice paddle. That is not paper, but it is in the letter too. And it tells them what they can let go without guilt. That is the part people forget. I wrote, you can throw away everything else. You do not need to read it. I already read it for you. When I wrote that sentence, my hand was shaking because I understood what a gift it would have been to read that sentence on the floor of my mother's house. Now I will tell you what was in the brown envelope, the one I almost put in the bag. Inside was one sheet of paper, folded in three, in my mother's handwriting. It was a list, eleven lines. On each line, one thing in the house and the name of who should have it. The tansu, for Kenji. The kimono, with the cranes, for Sachiko. Her sewing box, for the neighbor, Mrs. Ieda, who taught her to sew. the little Buddhist altar for Kenji's son.

Eleven things. Eleven lines. The only time my mother told us what mattered. We found it on day nine. By day nine, two of the eleven things were already gone. Her sewing box went to a donation truck on day four, and her good umbrella with the bamboo handle for her sister's daughter went to the curb in a bag. Two of eleven, gone, because her one important paper was hidden at the bottom of a drawer full of unimportant paper. That is why, dear, the letter must say, open this first, and it must be on top, and your children must know where it is. This is what I do at 80. Every year on my birthday, I read my letter, and I change what has changed, and I add one new memory, one little story about something in the house. Last year I wrote about the teapot with the chipped lid, and how Tom chipped it in 1976 and was afraid to tell me for a week.

Now my daughter wants that teapot more than anything. Before the letter, it was a chipped teapot. Now it has a story, and the story will stay. Let me give you my whole paper week, so you can start this Monday, very small. Monday, 15 minutes. Magazines and catalogs, one bag out the door. Tuesday, 15 minutes. The manual drawer, walk with it from room to room. Wednesday, receipts. The clear pocket on the refrigerator, the shredder. Thursday, cards, one per person, the address book. Friday, the someday shelf, the pencil dates. Saturday, rest or bake the cake from the recipe. Sunday, the basket from the genkan, the tea, and one hour with the blue folder or with your letters. Every day of the week, two minutes at the door with the mail. In one month, you will not recognize your drawers.

Some of you asked me questions in the comments of my last video about the house, and I want to answer two here, because they are about paper. Margaret wrote, Sachiko, my husband will not let me throw away anything with his name on it. Dear Margaret, start with your own papers, not his. When he sees your drawer close all the way, he will ask you how you did it. That is how Tom started. He watched me for one month and then he asked for his own grocery bag and his own timer. And Linda wrote, What if my children say they want everything? Ask them to come and choose now while you are here, one Saturday with lunch. Most children who say I want everything take three things when they see the boxes and the three things they choose, write them in your letter. Then everybody knows. So here are the 11 rules again. one breath each, and you can write them on the back of an envelope.

1. Start with the paper that has no story. 2. Paper does not cross the Genkan without a decision. 3. The manuals go, except the ones that keep you safe and the ones under warranty. 4. A receipt has a short life, and the big questions go to your accountant. 5. Keep the person, not the pile of cards, one card per person. 6. One blue folder, a thin map of where things are. 7. Read the letters once more and choose 10 from each person. 8. Give the children their childhood back now with the stories. 9. Decide yourself what happens to your diaries. 10. The Sunday pile gets one shelf and a date. And 11. Write the letter that says, Open this first, and tell them which 10% to keep. My mother left us 41 bags of paper and one sheet with 11 lines. I wish it had been the other way around. Forty-one lines and one bag.

That is what season seri means to me now. It is not about throwing things away. It is about leaving behind a house where the important things are easy to find, so the people you love can spend their time remembering you, not searching for you. So tonight, only one thing, dear. Open that drawer, the one we opened together at the beginning. Take out one piece of paper that has no story and let it go. That is all. One. Tomorrow, two minutes at the door. And on your next birthday, write your letter. And tell me in the comments, what is the one thing in your house that you want your family to keep? Just one thing. I read every answer, and I will choose some for my next video. If you want the next step, watch my video about the 11 rules for the whole house. It is right here on the screen. My mother would have liked that one. Thank you for staying with me so long, dear.
Now go open the drawer. I will see you next week.
